summary.text: Writing each binomial coefficient at level \(p^r\) as its level-\(p^{r-1}\) counterpart times a product over residues not divisible by \(p\), the proof pairs \(i\) with \(p^r-i\) and expands; Faulhaber formulas and inversion of reduced residues give the extra divisibility of the reciprocal sums, while all higher terms vanish modulo the target power. The linear terms cancel using the inductively established auxiliary divisibility \(p^3\mid 2\binom{3p^j}{p^j}^2-9\binom{2p^j}{p^j}\), and an odd-prime unit factor is then cancelled to obtain the required modulus.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 C_3(n)=\binom{3n}{n},\qquad C_2(n)=\binom{2n}{n},
\]
so that
\[
 a(n)=C_3(n)^2-27C_2(n).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge2\),
\[
 a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]

Throughout the proof, for \(k\ge1\), put
\[
 I_k=\{i:1\le i\le p^k,\ p\nmid i\}.
\]
When calculations are made modulo a power of \(p\), every \(i\in I_k\), and also \(p^k-i\), is a unit, so expressions involving their reciprocals are meaningful.

## 1. Power sums on the nonmultiples of \(p\)

For \(e\ge1\), define the integer power sum
\[
 J_e(k)=\sum_{i\in I_k}i^e.
\]
Splitting the integers from \(1\) to \(p^k\) into multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\) gives
\[
 J_e(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{p^k}i^e-p^e\sum_{j=1}^{p^{k-1}}j^e. \tag{1}
\]
We shall need the cases \(e=2,4\). The standard formulas
\[
 6\sum_{i=1}^n i^2=n(n+1)(2n+1)
\]
and
\[
 30\sum_{i=1}^n i^4
 =n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1)
\]
follow, for example, by induction on \(n\). Substituting these formulas into (1), with \(n=p^k\) and \(n=p^{k-1}\), shows respectively that
\[
 p^k\mid 6J_2(k),\qquad p^k\mid 30J_4(k). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, after writing \(p^k=p\,p^{k-1}\), each difference has an explicit factor \(p^k\). For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
6J_2(k)
={}&p^k(p^k+1)(2p^k+1)\\
&-p^2p^{k-1}(p^{k-1}+1)(2p^{k-1}+1),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is visibly divisible by \(p^k\); the fourth-power formula works identically.

If \(k\ge2\), then
\[
 p\mid J_2(k),\qquad p\mid J_4(k). \tag{3}
\]
To see this, note that for a prime \(p\ge3\), neither \(6\) nor \(30\) is divisible by \(p^2\). Thus (2), which supplies at least two factors of \(p\), forces one factor of \(p\) into the corresponding \(J_e(k)\). This includes the exceptional possibilities \(p=3\) and \(p=5\), since each occurs only to the first power in \(6\) or \(30\).

We also use the following inverse-power observation. Reduction modulo \(p^k\) identifies inversion with a permutation of the numbers in \(I_k\): if \(i\in I_k\), the least positive residue of \(i^{-1}\pmod {p^k}\) again lies in \(I_k\), and inversion is an involution. Consequently, for every \(e\ge0\),
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_k}i^{-e}\equiv \sum_{i\in I_k}i^e\pmod {p^k}. \tag{4}
\]

Now define, in any quotient ring modulo a sufficiently large power of \(p\),
\[
 y_i=\frac1{i(p^k-i)},\qquad
 S_k=\sum_{i\in I_k}y_i,\qquad
 T_k=\sum_{i\in I_k}y_i^2.
\]
Modulo \(p^k\), since \(p^k-i\equiv-i\),
\[
 y_i\equiv-i^{-2},\qquad y_i^2\equiv i^{-4}.
\]
Using (4), we obtain
\[
 S_k\equiv-J_2(k),\qquad T_k\equiv J_4(k)\pmod {p^k}. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, (2) and (5) give
\[
 p^k\mid 6S_k, \tag{6}
\]
where this notation means that the corresponding divisibility holds in whatever quotient ring is being used. If \(k\ge2\), (3) and (5) also give
\[
 p\mid S_k,
 \qquad p\mid T_k. \tag{7}
\]

Let
\[
 U_k=\sum_{\substack{\{i,j\}\subset I_k\\i\ne j}}y_iy_j,
\]
where every unordered two-element subset is counted once. The elementary identity
\[
 2U_k=S_k^2-T_k \tag{8}
\]
shows, using (7), that
\[
 p\mid U_k\qquad(k\ge2), \tag{9}
\]
because \(2\) is invertible modulo every power of the odd prime \(p\).

We shall also need a weak version of (6) when \(k=1\):
\[
 p\mid180S_1. \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(p\), (5) says \(S_1\equiv-J_2(1)\), while (2) says \(p\mid6J_2(1)\). Multiplying by \(30\) proves (10).

## 2. Factorial-ratio product formulas

Let \(N=pM\), with \(M\ge1\), and put
\[
 I(N)=\{i:1\le i\le N,\ p\nmid i\}.
\]
Splitting the factorial \(N!\) into its factors divisible and not divisible by \(p\) gives
\[
 \left(\prod_{i\in I(N)}i\right)p^M M!=N!. \tag{11}
\]
Likewise, in the interval \(cN+1,\ldots,(c+1)N\), the multiples of \(p\) are exactly
\[
 p(cM+1),\ldots,p((c+1)M).
\]
Combining these decompositions with the factorial formulas for binomial coefficients yields
\[
 \binom{3N}{N}\prod_{i\in I(N)}i
 =\binom{3M}{M}\prod_{i\in I(N)}(2N+i), \tag{12}
\]
and
\[
 \binom{2N}{N}\prod_{i\in I(N)}i
 =\binom{2M}{M}\prod_{i\in I(N)}(N+i). \tag{13}
\]
For completeness, (12) follows by comparing
\((3N)!/(N!(2N)!)\) with \((3M)!/(M!(2M)!)\), using (11) for \(N!\), and splitting the interval \((2N,3N]\) into its multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\). Formula (13) is the same argument with the interval \((N,2N]\).

In a quotient ring modulo a power of \(p\), the product \(\prod_{i\in I(N)}i\) is a unit. We may therefore cancel it from (12) and (13). Since
\[
 2N+i=i\left(1+\frac{2N}{i}\right),\qquad
 N+i=i\left(1+\frac Ni\right),
\]
we obtain
\[
 C_3(N)=C_3(M)F_2(N),\qquad C_2(N)=C_2(M)F_1(N), \tag{14}
\]
where
\[
 F_2(N)=\prod_{i\in I(N)}\left(1+\frac{2N}{i}\right),
 \qquad
 F_1(N)=\prod_{i\in I(N)}\left(1+\frac Ni\right). \tag{15}
\]

## 3. Reflection and product expansions

Suppose now that \(N=p^k\). Reflection \(i\mapsto N-i\) is an involution of \(I_k\). For any scalar \(c\), direct multiplication gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(1+\frac{cN}{i}\right)
\left(1+\frac{cN}{N-i}\right)
&=1+\frac{cN\bigl(i+(N-i)\bigr)+c^2N^2}{i(N-i)}\\
&=1+(c+c^2)N^2y_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Reindexing one copy of the product by reflection therefore gives
\[
 \left(\prod_{i\in I_k}\left(1+\frac{cN}{i}\right)\right)^2
 =\prod_{i\in I_k}\left(1+(c+c^2)N^2y_i\right). \tag{16}
\]
Thus, with
\[
 d_2=6N^2,\qquad d_1=2N^2,
\]
we have
\[
 F_2(N)^2=\prod_{i\in I_k}(1+d_2y_i),\qquad
 F_1(N)^2=\prod_{i\in I_k}(1+d_1y_i). \tag{17}
\]

We repeatedly use the elementary expansion
\[
 \prod_i(1+z_i)
 =1+\sum_i z_i+\sum_{i<j}z_iz_j+\text{terms of degree at least three}. \tag{18}
\]
If every \(z_i\) is divisible by \(q^e\), where \(q\) denotes the residue class of \(p\), then the final group in (18) is divisible by \(q^{3e}\). In particular,
\[
 \prod_{i\in I_k}(1+dy_i)
 =1+dS_k+d^2U_k+R_d,\qquad q^{3e}\mid R_d, \tag{19}
\]
whenever \(q^e\mid d\).

Two useful consequences follow.

First,
\[
 q^{2k}\mid F_1(N)-1. \tag{20}
\]
Indeed, in the direct expansion of \(F_1(N)\), all terms of degree at least two contain \(N^2=q^{2k}\). For the linear term, reflection gives
\[
 2\sum_{i\in I_k}\frac1i
 =N\sum_{i\in I_k}\frac1{i(N-i)}=NS_k.

after summing the identity
\[
 \frac1i+\frac1{N-i}=\frac{N}{i(N-i)}.
\]
Hence, if \(X=N\sum i^{-1}\) is the linear term in \(F_1(N)-1\), then
\[
 2X=N^2S_k,
\]
which is divisible by \(q^{2k}\). Since \(2\) is a unit, so is \(X\), proving (20).

Second, from (17), every nonconstant term in \(F_2(N)^2\) contains \(d_2=6N^2\), and hence
\[
 q^{2k}\mid F_2(N)^2-1. \tag{21}
\]
If \(k\ge2\), the sharper estimate
\[
 q^{3k}\mid F_2(N)^2-1 \tag{22}
\]
holds. To prove it, use (19): the linear term is
\[
 d_2S_k=N^2(6S_k),
\]
which is divisible by \(q^{2k}q^k=q^{3k}\) by (6). The quadratic term is divisible by \(N^4=q^{4k}\), and the terms of degree at least three are divisible by \(q^{6k}\). Both exponents are at least \(3k\).

## 4. An auxiliary congruence modulo \(p^3\)

Define
\[
 D_j=2C_3(p^j)^2-9C_2(p^j).
\]
We claim that
\[
 p^3\mid D_j\qquad(j\ge0). \tag{23}
\]
We first prove that \(D_j\equiv D_{j-1}\pmod {p^3}\) for \(j\ge1\).

Work modulo \(p^3\), put
\[
 A=C_3(p^{j-1}),\qquad B=C_2(p^{j-1}),
\]
and let \(F_2,F_1\) be the products associated with \(N=p^j\). By (14),
\[
 D_j-D_{j-1}
 =2A^2(F_2^2-1)-9B(F_1-1). \tag{24}
\]
If \(j\ge2\), (21) and (20) show that both \(F_2^2-1\) and \(F_1-1\) are divisible by \(q^{2j}\), hence by \(q^3\), so (24) vanishes modulo \(p^3\).

It remains to handle \(j=1\). Then \(A=C_3(1)=3\) and \(B=C_2(1)=2\), so (24) becomes
\[
 K=18(F_2^2-1)-18(F_1-1).
\]
We shall prove that \(K\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\) after multiplying by the unit \(F_1+1\). Algebraically,
\[
\begin{aligned}
K(F_1+1)
={}&18(F_2^2-1)(F_1-1)\\
&+\bigl(36(F_2^2-1)-18(F_1^2-1)\bigr). \tag{25}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term is divisible by \(q^4\), by (20) and (21) with \(j=1\).

For the parenthesized term, use (17) and (19), now with \(N=p\), \(d_2=6p^2\), and \(d_1=2p^2\). Its terms of degree at least three are divisible by \(q^6\). Its linear contribution is
\[
 (36d_2-18d_1)S_1=180p^2S_1,
\]
which is divisible by \(q^3\) by (10). Its quadratic contribution is
\[
 (36d_2^2-18d_1^2)U_1=1224p^4U_1,
\]
which is also divisible by \(q^3\). Therefore the parenthesized expression in (25) is divisible by \(q^3\), and so is \(K(F_1+1)\).

By (20), \(F_1-1\) is divisible by \(q^2\), hence is nilpotent modulo \(p^3\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is a unit, and therefore
\[
 F_1+1=2+(F_1-1)
\]
is a unit: a unit plus a commuting nilpotent is a unit. We can cancel \(F_1+1\), obtaining \(K\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\). Thus \(D_j\equiv D_{j-1}\pmod {p^3}\) also for \(j=1\).

Finally,
\[
 D_0=2\binom31^2-9\binom21=18-18=0.
\]
Induction proves (23).

## 5. The main high-order cancellation

Fix \(r\ge2\), and work modulo
\[
 p^E,\qquad E=3r+3.
\]
Write
\[
 N=p^r,
 \qquad A=C_3(p^{r-1}),
 \qquad B=C_2(p^{r-1}),

after reduction into this quotient ring. From (23),
\[
 q^3\mid 2A^2-9B. \tag{26}
\]

We first prove
\[
 q^E\mid 2A^2(F_2^2-1)-27B(F_1^2-1). \tag{27}
\]
Using (17) and (19), write
\[
 F_2^2-1=d_2S_r+d_2^2U_r+R_2,
\]
\[
 F_1^2-1=d_1S_r+d_1^2U_r+R_1,
\]
where \(d_2=6N^2\), \(d_1=2N^2\), and both remainders are divisible by \(q^{6r}\).

The combined remainder
\[
 2A^2R_2-27BR_1
\]
is divisible by \(q^{6r}\), and
\[
 6r\ge3r+3=E
\]
because \(r\ge1\).

The combined linear term factors as
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2A^2d_2-27Bd_1)S_r
&=(12A^2-54B)N^2S_r\\
&=(2A^2-9B)N^2(6S_r).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (26), the first factor supplies \(q^3\); \(N^2\) supplies \(q^{2r}\); and (6) says that \(6S_r\) supplies \(q^r\). Thus this term is divisible by
\[
 q^{3+2r+r}=q^{3r+3}=q^E.
\]

The combined quadratic term is
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2A^2d_2^2-27Bd_1^2)U_r
&=36(2A^2-3B)N^4U_r.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(N^4\) supplies \(q^{4r}\), and (9) supplies one further factor \(q\). Since
\[
 4r+1\ge3r+3
\]
for \(r\ge2\), this term too is divisible by \(q^E\). This proves (27).

Now define the expression whose vanishing is actually required:
\[
 L=A^2(F_2^2-1)-27B(F_1-1).
\]
Multiplying by \(F_1+1\) and rearranging gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(F_1+1)
={}&A^2(F_2^2-1)(F_1-1)\\
&+\bigl(2A^2(F_2^2-1)-27B(F_1^2-1)\bigr). \tag{28}
\end{aligned}
\]
By (22), \(F_2^2-1\) is divisible by \(q^{3r}\); by (20), \(F_1-1\) is divisible by \(q^{2r}\). Therefore the first term on the right of (28) is divisible by \(q^{5r}\), and
\[
 5r\ge3r+3
\]
for \(r\ge2\). The second term is divisible by \(q^E\) by (27). Hence
\[
 q^E\mid L(F_1+1). \tag{29}
\]

Again (20) shows that \(F_1-1\) is nilpotent modulo \(p^E\), while \(2\) is a unit. Thus
\[
 F_1+1=2+(F_1-1)
\]
is a unit. Cancelling it from (29) gives
\[
 L=0\pmod {p^E}. \tag{30}
\]

Finally, by the factorial-ratio identities (14),
\[
 C_3(p^r)=AF_2,
 \qquad C_2(p^r)=BF_1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})
&=(AF_2)^2-27BF_1-(A^2-27B)\\
&=A^2(F_2^2-1)-27B(F_1-1)\\
&=L.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equation (30) says exactly that this difference is divisible by
\(p^E=p^{3r+3}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge3\) and every integer \(r\ge2\), as required.
